# Task Brief: Port Raptor: Call of the Shadows (Sector 1) to HTML5

## 1. Goal

Port *Raptor: Call of the Shadows* (Apogee, 1994) — sector 1 only, the shareware
content — from the original DOS game to a browser game built with HTML5 canvas,
vanilla JavaScript, and the Web Audio API. The port must render real game assets
(graphics and sounds) extracted from the original shareware data files, either at
build time or at runtime — no placeholder art, no placeholder audio. Do not use
any external frameworks or libraries beyond what ships in the browser (no React,
Phaser, PixiJS, Howler, etc.). A small vanilla test runner is fine if you want
one, but it is not required.

## 2. Worktree Layout

Your worktree root (`./`) contains the GPL C/ASM source of the original DOS game,
provided for reference and porting purposes, under `SOURCE/`, `GFX/`, `audiolib/`,
and `apodmx/`. It also contains the original shareware game data files under
`./data/` — GLB archive files, the shareware `RAP.EXE` for reference, and whatever
else the shareware distribution contained.

Build your web port as new files alongside/above this existing tree (for example
`index.html`, an asset-extraction or build script, and your JS source), and keep
the original source tree intact for reference — do not delete or rewrite it.

You must write and maintain a `README` documenting a working dev-server command
(for example `npx serve .`, `python -m http.server`, or similar) so that the port
can be opened and played in a browser at any milestone. Keep this command accurate
and working as you go — it will be used to check your progress at each milestone.

## 3. Standing Rules

- Vanilla JavaScript + HTML5 canvas + Web Audio API only. No external runtime
  frameworks or libraries. A lightweight bundler or dev-only tool is fine if it
  produces plain output, but avoid dependency-heavy tooling.
- Always leave behind a documented, working dev server command that serves a
  working build.
- Commit to git after completing each milestone (M1 through M5, below), so
  progress is checkpointed.
- Sector 1 (shareware) content only — you do not need to support later sectors
  or the registered/full game.

## 4. Milestone Ladder (M1–M5)

This is the actual grading spec. Copied verbatim:

- **M1**: level-1 background + player ship rendered on canvas from the real GLB
  data. Graded by screenshot similarity (SSIM) to a reference DOSBox frame on the
  playfield region (target >= 0.80), and >= 90% of the reference color palette
  present.
- **M2**: arrow keys move the ship; firing spawns a projectile.
- **M3**: wave-1 enemies spawn; a projectile hit decrements enemy HP or removes
  the enemy; the player can die.
- **M4**: HUD (score/shields) renders; a Web Audio context is running and at
  least one sound effect is triggered on firing.
- **M5**: the sector-1 loop completes — the wave counter advances through wave 9
  and a sector-complete screen appears.

## 5. Grader Interface Contract

You **must** implement exactly this. An automated Playwright script checks
against it — this is a hard requirement, not a suggestion.

- A canvas element `<canvas id="raptor-canvas">` whose internal pixel buffer is
  exactly 320x200 (`canvas.width === 320`, `canvas.height === 200`), independent
  of any CSS display scaling.
- Controls: `ArrowUp` / `ArrowDown` / `ArrowLeft` / `ArrowRight` move the ship;
  the Space bar fires. Use standard `keydown`/`keyup` DOM listeners — no custom
  input hook needed.
- A live-updated global object `window.__raptor` with this exact shape:

  ```js
  window.__raptor = {
    ready: boolean,            // true once the first frame (background + player ship) is drawn from real game data
    player: { x: number, y: number, alive: boolean },
    projectiles: [ { x: number, y: number, owner: 'player'|'enemy' }, /* ... */ ],
    enemies: [ { id: string|number, hp: number, x: number, y: number, alive: boolean }, /* ... */ ],
    hud: { score: number, shields: number },
    audio: { contextState: 'running'|'suspended'|'closed', sfxCount: number },  // sfxCount increments on every SFX triggered
    wave: number,               // current wave within sector 1
    sectorComplete: boolean
  };
  ```

- Keep this object's fields in sync with actual game state at all times. The
  grader polls it, drives real keyboard input to test M2/M3/M4/M5, and takes a
  canvas screenshot to test M1. For M5 the grader is allowed to auto-play (hold
  fire, jitter movement) rather than requiring skilled play, so you do not need
  to build any special "autoplay" or "god mode" feature — just make the interface
  accurately reflect real game state during ordinary play.

</file>

displayContent.text:
# DOS Raptor
This is the original Raptor Call Of The Shadows DOS source code v1.2 with the Apogee Sound System and the
DMX wrapper APODMX instead of the proprietary DMX library.

## Build
To build all libraries and the exe under DOS use Watcom C 10.0 and TASM 3.1.
For a build that more closely matches the original exe file v1.2 (without DMX library) you will need the following:
```
AUDIOLIB: Watcom C 10.0 and TASM 3.1
APODMX: A compatible version of Watcom C32 
GFX: Watcom C 9.5b and TASM 3.1
SOURCE: Watcom C 10.0 and TASM 3.1
```

## License
DOS Raptor is distributed under the GPL Version 2 or newer, see [LICENSE](https://github.com/skynettx/dosraptor/blob/master/LICENSE).

## Thanks
All my thanks go to [Scott Host](https://www.mking.com), [nukeykt](https://github.com/nukeykt) and [NY00123](https://github.com/NY00123) without them this release would not have been possible.

Now I have the GLB item map in hand. The key items for the game:

- FILE0000.GLB: text, music, SFX (Apogee Sound System format — .APF? Actually it's the old Apogee sound format: a header of 52 bytes containing rate, volume, loop, type, data)
- FILE0001.GLB:
  - 0x10000: palette (768 bytes of VGA palette)
  - 0x10001: SYSTEM_FNT font
  - 0x10022: BACKGRND_PIC — background image!
  - Fonts, numbers (N0-N9, N$), SHLDLOW_PIC (shields low?)
  - SPRITE1_ITM (0x100fc) — sprite library (SPRITE array)
  - FLATSG1_ITM (0x100fd) — flat library (FLATS array)
  - MAP1G1_MAP..MAP9G1_MAP (0x100fe-0x10106) — 9 waves of MAZELEVEL data!
  - SHIP01G1_PIC.. — sprite graphics (GFX_PIC)
  - STARTG1TILES..ENDG1TILES label — ground tiles (flat graphics)

So the "waves" are literally 9 MAP files (MAP1G1_MAP - MAP9G1_MAP) — 9 waves per sector! This matches M5's "the wave counter advances through wave 9".

The MAZELEVEL struct contains `map[MAP_SIZE]`, where MAP_SIZE = 150*9 = 1350 MAZEDATA entries, each 4 bytes (2 shorts) = 5400 bytes + 12-byte header. Each MAZEDATA: flats index, fgame.

Wait, but MAP_ROWS=150, MAP_COLS=9: the map is a scrolling vertical strip. The playfield is 320x200, and the map scrolls downward (the player flies upward). The visible area is 8x9 = 72 cells? MAP_ONSCREEN=8, MAP_COLS=9. Each cell is 32x32 px. 9 cols * 32 = 288 px = MAP_RIGHT-MAP_LEFT (304-16=288). 8 rows * 32 = 256 > 200-18… hmm, MAP_BOTTOM=182, MAP_TOP=2, height 180 px.

Let me look at RAP.C's Do_Game and ENEMY.C to understand wave loading and spawning. The MAZEDATA.flats field references an index into flatlib (FLATS array). FLATS.linkflat is a link to the next cell in the same flat group? Let me actually read ENEMY_C to understand.

Also, I need to understand how the map scrolls: the game has a "map" that scrolls down as the player advances. The MAP1G1 map has 150 rows of 9 columns. The 8 rows on screen. The top row of the visible window advances with the player's y position? Actually, in Raptor the player moves within a fixed vertical band (PLAYERINITY=160, MAXPLAYERY=160, MINPLAYERY=0), and the map scrolls down past the player.

Let me read ENEMY.C — this is the core: ENEMY_Think, ENEMY_LoadLib, ENEMY_InitSprites, and how enemies are spawned from the map.

I'll also read RAP.C (main loop, wave transitions, player display).

These are large files. Let me read ENEMY.C.
Continuing to read ENEMY.C.

Main logic:
- `tiley = (tilepos / MAP_COLS) - 3` — the top row on the screen corresponds to map row (tilepos/MAP_COLS)-3.
- Spawning: while cur_enemy->y == tiley, if level matches the difficulty, ENEMY_Add it and move cur_enemy forward (need to check the loop at lines 704-718).

ENEMY_Add:
- `new->y = tileyoff - ((tiley - sprite->y) * 32) - 97;` — here tileyoff is probably the player's y position (the y-offset of the map relative to the screen). The player is at screen y=160? So the map scrolls with the player: tileyoff = player's y position. The enemy's map row sprite->y is relative: screen_y = tileyoff - (tiley - sprite->y)*32 - 97. If tileyoff = player_cy? Let me check tileyoff in RAP.C.
- `new->x = (sprite->x * 32) + MAP_LEFT + 16 - hlx` etc.

GLB format:
- File header: KEYFILE struct (32 bytes: DWORD opt, DWORD offset, DWORD filesize, char name[16]) encrypted with key "32768GLB", SEED=0x19.
- `offset` after decryption = number of items in the file.
- Item table at offset 32: for each item, a KEYFILE struct (32 bytes each): opt (flags: ITF_LOCKED 0x80000000, ITF_ENCODED 0x40000000, GLB_NORMAL=0/GLB_ENCODED=1), offset into the file, filesize, name[16].

  - For GSPRITE (sprite): opt1 = number of rows, opt2 = total pixel count, followed by rows of (GFX_SPRITE: x, y, offset, length) 16 bytes each, then the pixel data.

Shadow: The aerial shadow is 3D perspective (GFX_3DPoint via G3D_SetView(160,100,1000)), which shades a 1px strip below the sprite using sdtable (palette -6 light). Ground shadow: directly darkens the sprite shape (GFX_ShadeShape DARK). GFX_Shade: for each pixel in the row, applies a shading table to the "display" pixel (not the sprite). So the shadow is: for the rows of each sprite, shade the terrain pixels at the projected position.

GFX_3DPoint: need to read it to reproduce the projection. It's in GFXAPI.C. Let's grep.

FLAME_Down: draws a vertical strip of width `width` (4) below the ship, with height 8 or 12 (frame%2), shading the display buffer with a light table (stable[num]) — the flame "brightens" the pixels it passes over?? GFX_Shade(displaybuffer, width, table) — applies a table to the display buffer's pixels (terrain). stable[n] = MakeLightTable(palette, (8-n)*2) → brighter colors. So the flame brightens the terrain pixels below the engine — interesting. The flame is not a sprite, it's a shading pass on the terrain.

# Raptor HTML5 Port — Plan & Progress

## Context
Port Raptor: Call of the Shadows (shareware, sector 1) to HTML5 canvas + vanilla JS +
Web Audio, using real assets extracted from `data/FILE0000.GLB` and `data/FILE0001.GLB`.
Graded via Playwright against `window.__raptor` (see brief). M1-M5 milestones, commit each.

## Research (done)
- GLB: 128B header + 54-byte item index (name[16], size u32, offset u32), little-endian. Verified.
- GFX_PIC: 20B header {type u32, opt1 u32, opt2 u32, w i32, h i32}.
  - type 0 (SPRITE): rows of 16B {x i32, y i32, offset i32 (unused for layout), len i32} + len pixels, until offset==0xFFFFFFFF.
  - type 1 (DENSE): w*h pixels inline.
- MAP item (MAZEDATA): {size u32, spriteoff u32, numsprites u32, MAZEDATA map[1350] u32 each {flats, fgame}} then numsprites×24B CSPRITE {link i32, slib i32, x i32, y i32, game i32, level i32}. MAP1G1_MAP = 12588B (299 csprites). Verified.
- SPRITE lib (SPRITE1_ITM, 528B entries ×131) & FLATS lib (FLATSG1_ITM, 8B entries ×672). Verified.
- SFX: 8B header {type u16(=3), rate u16 (11025), datasz u32} + 8-bit unsigned PCM (center 128). Digital variant = FX_LABEL+4. Verified across all FX groups.
- Game rules (from source): new player = forward guns + 75 shield + 10000 score; 9 waves
  (MAP{1..9}G1_MAP), 1px/frame scroll @ 23.33Hz tick (70Hz framecount, 3 per tick);
  enemy spawn when tiley==csprite->y; wave ends at end-marker + last enemy removed
  (startendwave=60 flyoff); death: shield<=0 → explosion at startendwave==24;
  shield bar x=308 (4px wide, 100 levels, colors 74..66), score = 8 digit sprites at (119,2);
  fonts in FILE0001 (SYSTEM_FNT/GAME_FNT: 772B header + packed bitmaps, char pixel = mask+basecolor).

## Build steps
- [x] Research formats & game logic
- [ ] M1: tools/extract.js → assets/raptor.bin + assets/index.json (palette, sprites,
      tiles G1 (all 4 flat libs for safety), sprite libs 1-4, maps 1-9, fonts, SFX PCM).
      js/raptor.js: asset loader, palette, sprite/tile blit, initial frame
      (tiles + player + HUD). index.html + README dev-server command.
- [ ] M2: keyboard movement (arrows, acceleration model) + Space fire (dual forward guns,
      projectiles, shot anims, sfx).
- [ ] M3: enemy spawn/AI (F_KAMI paths, F_GROUND), enemy shots (ESHOT types),
      player/enemy/shot collisions, HP, explosions, player death + retry.
- [ ] M4: HUD (score/shields/weapons, low-shield warning), Web Audio context,
      SFX on fire/hit/explosion (sfxCount counter).
- [ ] M5: wave transitions (landing screen), wave 9 → sector-complete screen,
      full loop, commits.

## Dev server
`python -m http.server 8000` from repo root (or `npx serve .`) → http://localhost:8000

## Notes / decisions
- No menus: page loads straight into wave 1 (normal diff) so grader sees playfield immediately.
- Death: after explosion, short death screen, auto-restart same wave after ~4s (score→start_score,
  shield→75). Keeps M5 auto-play (hold fire) from stalling.
- Fade-in skipped; first frame full brightness (SSIM vs reference).
- Timing: fixed 23.33Hz logic tick via rAF accumulator (authentic pace: 1px/tick scroll).
- __raptor.player.x/y = ship top-left (playerx/playery); projectiles/enemies = top-left sprite coords;
  enemies array = active enemies (alive:true).

The GLB parser exists and works. Next, write `tools/extract.js`.

Design of `assets/raptor.bin` + `assets/index.json`:

index.json:
```json
{
  "palette": [768 bytes as array],
  "bin": {
    "name": "raptor.bin",
    "entries": {
       "LPLAYER_PIC": {"off": n, "size": m, "w": .., "h": .., "type": 0|1, "file": 0},
       ...
    }
  },
  "sfx": { "GUN": {"off":..., "rate":11025, "len":...}, ... }
}
```
Hmm — sfx can go inside the same bin as an entry with kind:"sfx". Keep a single entry table keyed by name:
- kind: "gfx" (raw GFX_PIC bytes), "sfx" (raw: 8B header + pcm), "map" (raw MAZEDATA), "lib" (raw), "font" (raw font bytes), "pal", "text".
Everything is just raw item bytes stored in order; the runtime decodes per kind based on name/kind hints.

Entry naming: for FILE0000, items that have no name get a name from the label: use label names where they exist; for unnamed data items between labels, generate a name like "FX0091" (item number in hex). The runtime looks up what it needs by name:
- Sprites: exact names from FILE0000.INC / FILE0001.INC (LPLAYER_PIC, NMSHOT_BLK, ESHOT_BLK, BONUS00_PIC, GEXPLO_BLK, SMFLAK_BLK, BOOM_PIC, SPLAT_BLK, BIGSPLAT_BLK, LGFLAK_BLK, EXPLO2_BLK, AIRBOOM_PIC, NRGBANG_BLK, LRBLST_BLK, SSMOKE_BLK, SMOKTRAL_BLK, LGHTIN_BLK, BSPARK_BLK, OSPARK_BLK, GUNSTR_BLK, FLARE_PIC, SPARKLE_PIC, SHIPGLOW_BLK, ELASEPOW_BLK, DETHPOW_BLK, LASERPOW_BLK, DRAYHIT_BLK, PLASMA_BLK, MICROM_BLK, MISDUM_BLK, MISRAT_BLK, MISGRD_BLK, BLDGBOMB_PIC, POWDIS_BLK, MEGABM_BLK, SHOKWV_BLK, FRNTLAS_BLK, DETHRY_BLK, EMISLE_BLK, MINE_BLK, ELASER_BLK, EPLASMA_PIC, COCONUT_PIC, ICNGLW_BLK, SHLDLOW_PIC, WEPDEST_PIC, SMSHIELD_PIC, SMBOMB_PIC, N0_PIC..N9_PIC, NS_PIC, STARTG1TILES.., SPRITE1_ITM..SPRITE4_ITM, FLATSG1_ITM..FLATSG4_ITM, MAP1G1_MAP..MAP9G1_MAP, PALETTE_DAT, SYSTEM_FNT, GAME_FNT, FONT1_FNT, FONT2_FNT, END0_TXT.., ORDER_TXT, LPLAYER_PIC+? — note: frames of LPLAYER_PIC are separate items LPLAYER_PIC..LPLAYER_PIC+6 (7 items: 0x11a..0x120? From FILE0001.INC: LPLAYER_PIC 0x11a=282; +1..+6 = 283..288 — do these have names? In the .INC, only the first one is defined (LPLAYER_PIC). The others are unnamed items. So we have to include unnamed items and name them by index.

Therefore: the extractor includes all items from both GLBs except music, and names unnamed items as "f0_XXXX" / "f1_XXXX" (file + hex item number). The index records all entries by name, and the runtime code references frames by the base name and +1..n computed from the item index (the index also stores the numeric item index: "idx": 282 → frame item name = f0/f1 name of idx+1...). Better approach: the extractor generates explicit names for all frames of known block bases: for a base B with F frames (known list), include items B..B+F-1 under names like "LPLAYER_PIC+1"? JSON keys can be anything. Cleaner: entries keyed by base name, with a "frames": [ {off, size}, ... ] array? The sizes/offsets are contiguous per item in my bin.

The simplest, most robust approach: an entries array (not object):
```
"items": [ {name, idx, off, size, kind, w, h, rate?} ... ]
```
Plus a "names" map: name → array index into items. And for frame sequences, the runtime uses item-index lookup: the index map is by name; frames of LPLAYER_PIC: the extractor adds explicit map entries: "LPLAYER_PIC_0".."LPLAYER_PIC_6"? That requires hardcoding the frame counts — no problem, I know them (player 7, NMSHOT 4, etc.). Actually, a simpler generic method: for every named block base in the .INC that is followed by unnamed items, the extractor automatically adds entries: if an unnamed item's index is between named label N (idx i) and the next named item (idx j), name it `<N>+<k>` (k = idx-i). Example: LPLAYER_PIC+1, LPLAYER_PIC+4 (player frames 1..4 = LPLAYER_PIC+1..+4? wait, frames: LPLAYER_PIC+0..+6 are 7 items — but item 289 (LPLAYER_PIC+7) is a different sprite? In the .INC: after LPLAYER_PIC 0x11a there's SHIP01G1_PIC 0x11f=287 → so LPLAYER_PIC+0..+5 (6 frames: 282..286), then 287 = SHIP01G1_PIC. Hmm! 6 frames? But the ship has 7 pics (0..6). Let me recheck FILE0001.INC: LPLAYER_PIC 0x11a (282), SHIP01G1_PIC 0x11f (287) → 287-282 = 5 → frames 0..4 (5 items). Hmm, but playerpic goes 0..6 (7 values: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6). And SHIP01G1_PIC 0x11f, next? Let me look at the FILE0001.INC listing around those entries. From the earlier archive: "LPLAYER_PIC 0x11a //ITEM:282" "SHIP01G1_PIC 0x11f //ITEM:287". And curship[loop] = LPLAYER_PIC + loop for loop 0..6 → LPLAYER_PIC+5 = 287 = SHIP01G1_PIC, +6 = 288! So the 7 ship pics are: LPLAYER_PIC, +1, +2, +3, +4, SHIP01G1_PIC, SHIP01G1_PIC+1.
